newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish end-Jan private sector credit growth 15.2 pc.
newsitem.headline: Irish end-Jan private sector credit growth 15.2 pc.

text.p: The adjusted annual growth rate of Irish private sector credit rose to 15.2 percent at the end of January from 14.7 percent at the end of December, central bank data showed on Thursday.
The increase in residential mortgage lending was slightly lower than in January 1996 resulting in a slight drop in the annual rate to 14 percent from 14.1 percent in December, it said.
Residential mortgage lending increased by 60 million Irish pounds with most of the increase being advanced by building societies, it said. Other mortgages fell by 14 million pounds.

Non-mortage Irish pound credit fell in January but by less than in the same month last year. As a result, the annual rate of increase rose to 16.9 percent in January from 16.5 percent in December, it said.
The adjusted annual rate of money supply growth fell to 14.7 percent from 15.7 percent, the central bank said.
Private sector credit increased by 548 million Irish pounds or 1.6 percent in January, but 543 million of this was due to foreign-currency lending to non IFSC entities, the central bank said.
It said that private sector credit data contrasted with a fall in January 1996, "which largely accounts for the pick-up in the annual adjusted rate of credit growth."

Credit to the government fell by 137 million Irish pounds in January. Non-residents increased their holdings of Irish government securities by 129 million during the month while holdings of domestic credit institutions fell.

Positive Irish-pound funding added to EU receipts exceeded net Government expenditure and payments on the Exchequer foreign debt, contributing to an increase of 15 million pounds in government balances at the central bank," it said.
The official external reserves rose by 808 million Irish pounds in January, the central bank said.
It said positive foreign-exchange market interventions, EU receipts and a valuation adjustment of 120 million Irish pounds were the main factors accounting for this increase.
